https://www.cosmopolitan.com/style-beaut.text: Taking a trip down beauty memory lane is equal parts cringe and endearing. While looking back on my ombré hair of 2012 and silver smokey eye of 2016 might send a shiver down my spine today, they were simply moments in time you had to be there for. But one category whose trends have evolved, while still holding up decades later, is undoubtedly manicures.From the days of strolling down the aisles of CVS to pick up Mint Candy Apple for my next chaotic design endeavor, to now being a beauty editor who gets to write about nail trends every day, a lot has changed. Thick glitter polishes have transformed into shiny chrome finishes, while crackle and marble manis have made their way back to our fingers as a reminiscent throwback.If you’re feeling a nostalgic yearning for the good old days, you can actually try many of these designs again without fully reverting to your middle-school self. Consider this your guide to the nail trends that defined different beauty eras, with plenty of elevated takes worth trying today.Marble NailsI have vivid memories of coming home after school in sixth grade and sitting at my kitchen table trying to master the art of marble nails. I would meticulously drop polish into a red solo cup and swirl with a toothpick until my desired pattern appeared. It’s safe to say that my 11-year-old mani did not turn out nearly as cute as the marble inspiration below, but the nostalgia still stands.Thick French TipsTo this day, my mom still rocks a thick French tip, and for context she’s the chicest person I know. Deep French was super popular in the ’90s and early aughts, and has seen a recent revival (as proven by Kylie rocking them below) in recent years. Just choose a sheer pinky base and a bright white polish for the thick tip, and the result is an edgy take on the classic.Crackle NailsCrackle nails bring me straight back to middle school, and last year Sally Hansen brought the polish back from the manicure graveyard. For the unfamiliar, paint your favorite color(s) as a base, then coat the crackle polish on top and watch as it separates to create a fractured effect. And there you go, it’s basically 2012 again and you’re ready for Tumblr fame.Colorblock NailsIf you were a fan of colorblock nails back in the day, good news: The trend is just as fun to recreate now, whether you opt for a full rainbow, a tonal gradient, or a combination of completely mismatched shades on each nail. The key to making the throwback look feel a little more elevated? Choose polishes with a shiny or milky finish that give each finger some depth. It’s cute without looking like you pulled out your dried-up nail polish collection from elementary school.Glitter PolishIt’s important that chrome and cat-eye finishes remember their roots—glitter nails. Nearly blinding sparkly fingers were a mainstay in the 2000s, from subtle pinks to bright neons, and honestly, we’re seeing a revival apropos of launches from big salon brands like Apres Nail’s Enigmatic line and OPI’s Infinite Shine.Accent NailsIt was a girlhood rite of passage going to the nail salon for your first manicure and getting a single-nail design, specifically a tropical flower on the ring finger. While there are definitely playful ways to elevate an accent finger, the sentiment still remains, airbrush patterns and all.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/17/iran.text: Tehran has ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave Iranian territory within 48 hours, after Sweden expelled an Iranian diplomat from its embassy in Stockholm on Wednesday over activities described as incompatible with diplomatic norms.Alireza Yousofi, director-general for Western Europe at Iran's foreign ministry, summoned the Swedish ambassador in Tehran on Thursday to deliver the reciprocal expulsion order and convey what he described as Iran's protest at Sweden's "destructive policies and its hosting of terrorist groups."Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement that Sweden's decision to restrict the activities of an Iranian diplomat was "baseless" and attributed it to alleged Israeli influence, describing the move as an attempt to disrupt normal operations at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.Tehran warned that any disruption of the embassy's work would engage Sweden's international responsibility under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.Sweden's foreign ministry had summoned the Iranian ambassador in Stockholm on Wednesday and ordered the expulsion of one of his embassy's diplomats, citing "improper activities incompatible with the Vienna Convention." It gave no further details of what those activities involved.Sweden and Iran have a history of diplomatic confrontations. In June 2024, two Swedish citizens, Johan Floderus and Saeed Azizi, were released in a prisoner swap in exchange for Hamid Nouri, a former Iranian prison official who had been serving a life sentence in Sweden.Nouri was arrested at Stockholm Airport in November 2019 under universal jurisdiction and convicted for his role in the mass execution of political prisoners in Iran in 1988.In July 2025, Sweden joined several European countries, the US and Canada in accusing Tehran of orchestrating plots to threaten, abduct and harass dissidents, journalists and activists abroad.

Photograph: Nacho Doce/Reuters France More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last week Europe live – latest updates Rory Carroll Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.08 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for a second week of student protests. Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday. The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray. Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations and erected barricades last week to protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system. View image in fullscreen Students block the entrance to Ampere high school in Lyon. Photograph: Konrad K/Sipa/Shutterstock Clashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration. There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”. Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on 17 September and spread across the capital and the rest of France. “There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.” The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray. The protests caught the government by surprise and confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Security forces are stationed at Place de la Nation in Paris on Friday during the student protests. Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Student grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms during heatwaves . Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff. The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher, 59, was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday. The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day of strikes last week to compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week.
